questions.stem: Which multiplication has the same answer as 2 + 2 + 2 + 2?
questions.stemText: Which multiplication has the same answer as 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 ?
questions.explain: Count the 2s: there are 4 of them, so this is 4 groups of 2, which is 4 × 2 = 8. Counting one group too many gives 5 × 2, which is 2 too much, and multiplying the wrong pair gives 2 × 2 or 5 × 4. Multiplication is a short way of writing the same number added over and over - that is the whole idea, and it is why the times tables are worth knowing by heart.

questions.stem: Farhan works out 6842 + 2830 in columns. One column makes 16, so he writes 6 in that column and a small 1 above the column on its left. How much is the 6 he writes there worth?
questions.stemText: Farhan works out 6842 + 2830 in columns. One column makes 16, so he writes 6 in that column and a small 1 above the column on its left. How much is the 6 he writes there worth?
questions.explain: The column that makes 16 is the hundreds column: 8 + 8 = 16, and no other column reaches ten. 16 hundreds is 1 thousand and 6 hundreds, so the 6 stays in the hundreds column - worth 600 - and the small 1 goes above the thousands column - worth 1000. The 6 is worth 600. A mark is worth the column it is written in, not the digit it looks like: that is what regrouping means, ten of something small becoming one of the next size up. Every wrong answer here is one of the two slips - the right digit read in the wrong column, or the wrong digit read in the right one.

questions.stemText: Jun Hao makes a pattern of figures with toothpicks. Figure 1: 5 toothpicks Figure 2: 12 toothpicks Figure 3: 19 toothpicks Figure 4: 26 toothpicks The pattern goes on in the same way. How many more toothpicks does Figure 12 use than Figure 8?
questions.explain: Find the jump first: 5 → 12 → 19 → 26, so each figure uses 7 more toothpicks than the one before. From Figure 8 to Figure 12 there are 12 − 8 = 4 jumps, and each jump adds 7 toothpicks: 4 × 7 = 28. You do not need to work out either figure. (Check: Figure 8 uses 54 and Figure 12 uses 82; 82 − 54 = 28.)

questions.stem: Wei Ling lays 4 identical rectangular tiles side by side in one row. Together they make a rectangle 36 cm long and 10 cm wide. What is the area of one tile?
questions.stemText: Wei Ling lays 4 identical rectangular tiles side by side in one row. Together they make a rectangle 36 cm long and 10 cm wide. What is the area of one tile?
questions.explain: The 4 tiles share the 36 cm length equally, so each tile measures 36 ÷ 4 = 9 cm along the row. Its other side is as wide as the whole row: 10 cm. Area of one tile = 9 × 10 = 90 cm². (The whole rectangle is 36 × 10 = 360 cm², and 360 ÷ 4 = 90 cm² too.)

Along that side there is 6 cm of edge before the notch and 6 cm after it, and the banner is still 8 cm wide behind the notch. Every corner is a right angle. What is the perimeter of the banner now?
questions.explain: Walk the eight sides: 6 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 6 + 10 + 18 + 10 = 60 cm. Careful: this notch is in the middle of a side, not at a corner. The 6 cm taken out of the top edge is replaced by the 6 cm along the bottom of the notch, so that part of the walk is unchanged. But the two sides of the notch, 2 cm down and 2 cm back up, are brand new. Perimeter = 2 × (18 + 10) + 2 × 2 = 60 cm. A corner cut leaves the perimeter alone; a middle notch makes it longer.
